article.title: Year-End Close: The Four-Week Runway That Makes January Boring
article.body_markdown:
Every January, thousands of small businesses re-learn the same lesson: the year did not end on December 31 in their books — it ended somewhere in late February, after six weeks of shoeboxes, half-reconciled bank statements, and an accountant asking for one more thing. The cost is not just the late nights: December's numbers stay provisional for two months, the year's true margin is unknown exactly when annual decisions need it, and every January decision is made on November's data with December's stress.

The fix is not working harder in January. It is a **runway that starts December 1**: four dates, each with a short list, each owned by name. Projects with owners and dates finish; projects with intentions do not.

## The four dates

1. **December 1 — open the runway.** One meeting, thirty minutes, one output: the checklist with a name and a date on every line. Request contractor and vendor year-end statements now — slow suppliers answer in January if you ask in January, but in December they answer in December.
2. **December 15 — the pre-close.** Reconciliations current through November, AR aging started, bad-debt list drafted, prepaids and fixed-asset register pulled, and the "things we know are wrong but have been avoiding" list written down honestly. Mid-December is the last point where problems are cheap.
3. **December 31 — the hard cutoff.** Final bank and card reconciliations to the 31st, physical inventory counted and valued, December invoiced, ledger cut off. A close that stays open "just this once" is a close that never happened.
4. **First two weeks of January — adjustments, then lock.** Depreciation, accruals, prepaids, write-downs, provision, payroll year end. Then lock the period: no retro edits. Locked books make this year comparable to every other year.

## The eleven-item checklist (every line has an owner and a date)

1. Bank and credit-card reconciliations, all accounts, through December 31
2. AR aging, line by line — collect in December what December can collect
3. AP complete and cut off — the missing December liability overstates profit
4. Physical inventory count and valuation — shrink found in December is a line item, not a tax surprise
5. Fixed-asset register reconciled, depreciation posted
6. Payroll year end — final run reconciled, summaries prepared
7. Contractor and vendor summaries — late or missing ones are the cheapest-to-avoid, most-commonly-paid fines in small business
8. Prepaid expenses and accruals — the item that makes this December comparable to last December
9. Bad-debt provision, decided once, with a reason attached
10. Loans and interest reconciled to the cutoff date
11. Document retention and the closing binder — next year's runway, pre-built

## Three honesty rules

- **Reconcile to the bank, not to the plan.** Every adjustment gets a reason a stranger could read.
- **Never fix January's numbers with December's entries.** A close that can be reopened for convenience was never closed — it was paused, and every number downstream inherits the doubt.
- **Close the books and lock them.** The lock is what makes "this year vs last year" a measurement instead of a memory.

## The five traps

The January crawl (December work done in January takes three times longer) · the shoebox December · the "we'll true it up later" retro-edit that kills the period lock forever · the skipped write-down that borrows from next year's credibility · the commingled owner account that debuts at year-end instead of at the monthly reconciliation.

## The contractor who stopped closing in February

A fourteen-person HVAC contractor closed its books in late February for years. The change was not software — it was the four-date runway. What the close itself found: **$14,200** of December service work installed but not invoiced (paperwork in a tech's truck), **$6,300** of inventory shrink that would otherwise have inflated profit into a tax bill, and a **$2,800** supplier bill never entered — roughly $20,500 of truth that January-them would have found at tax-prep speed, in March, as an argument with the accountant. Books locked January 12 instead of February 26, the CPA fee dropped, and the January 15 pricing decision was made on December's real margin instead of November's guess.

---

article.description: A four-date December runway, an eleven-item checklist with an owner on every line, three honesty rules, and five traps - plus the HVAC contractor who closed on January 12 instead of February 26.
